name: journal-did-rome-ban-gospels-in-382.json
content:
The claim comes in several forms. A council at Rome in 382 banned every gospel that disagreed with Paul, and the four we have were what was left. Samuel Davidson, who wrote a history of the canon in 1877, names no such council.1 He does report a list of books under the name of Pope Damasus, who held office from 366 to 384. That list is the nearest thing to a 382 story, and it is a different thing.

What Davidson reports

Davidson writes: "A canonical list appears in three different forms bearing the names of Damasus (366-384), Gelasius I. (492-496), and Hormisdas (514-523)."2 All three are lists of books to be received. None of them is a ruling that burned or banned a gospel.

In the Damasus form, he says, "The New Testament books are the four gospels, fourteen epistles of Paul, the Apocalypse, and Acts, with seven Catholic epistles."3 The Gelasian form is "almost identical with the preceding", and in the New Testament "the epistle to the Hebrews is absent."4

Davidson also records the doubt. "The MSS. of these lists present some diversity; and Credner supposes the Damasus-list a fiction. But Thiel has vindicated its authenticity."5 He allows that "some interpolations may exist in the last two", and that the first "may well belong to the time of Damasus." He sides with the list, and he still finds no council in it.

The Gelasian Decree

The text most often meant in these claims is the Decree of Gelasius. It carries the name of Gelasius I, who was pope from 492 to 496. That is more than a century after 382. In the form printed today it is usually dated to the sixth century, and scholars still argue about which parts are older.6

The Decree lists books to be received and books to be avoided. Whatever its date, it is a document about reading, written long after the four gospels were the church's standard. It does not describe a council in 382.

How the books were gathered

Davidson's own account of the process is slow and local. "When it is asked, to whom do we owe the canon? the usual answer is, to the Church. This is true only in a sense."7 Near the end he sums up the whole history: "No definite principles guided the course of its formation, or fixed its present state."8

The councils he does name are African. The synods of Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397 "received the epistle to the Hebrews and the seven general ones, thus fixing the New Testament canon as it now is."9 Carthage repeated the list in 419 with one change, fourteen letters of Paul where the earlier list had thirteen.10

What remains of the claim

Part of the claim is sound. Many more gospels circulated than the four, and churches did draw up lists of books to be read and books to be set aside. The site's own case, that Paul's letters shaped what the church kept, rests on the lists themselves: every list Davidson reports puts Paul's letters in.

The date and the council do not hold. The lists come from the late fourth century onward, from Latin sources and from African synods, and the Decree is later again. The site's article on the gospels has been corrected to say so.

Verdict. No council at Rome in 382 is shown to have banned the other gospels. The Damasus list is a list of books received, and the Gelasian Decree is a century later.
